reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the CNS
clinicalPearls: A well-differentiated glioneuronal tumour (usually CNS WHO grade 1) and a common cause of chronic drug-resistant focal epilepsy in children and young adults
Composed of both dysplastic neurons (ganglion cells) and a neoplastic glial component
Most often cortical and temporal, correlating with its strong association with focal seizures
MRI typically shows a circumscribed, often cystic lesion with a mural nodule, variable enhancement and frequent calcification
BRAF V600E mutation is common and can be exploited diagnostically and, in selected higher-grade cases, therapeutically
Diagnosis rests on recognising the abnormal ganglion cells; a well-formed glial component distinguishes it from lesions of pure neuronal or glial type
Complete surgical resection is usually curative and offers a high chance of seizure freedom
reference.pathophysiology: Ganglioglioma is a benign glioneuronal tumour containing a mixture of dysplastic, neoplastic ganglion (neuronal) cells and a neoplastic glial component, usually astrocytic. It commonly arises in the cerebral cortex, most often the temporal lobe, and grows slowly, frequently forming a cyst with a solid mural nodule. Activation of the MAP kinase signalling pathway, most characteristically through the BRAF V600E mutation, is a recurrent molecular event. The disorganised neuronal and glial architecture disrupts cortical circuitry and produces the chronic focal epilepsy that dominates presentation. Rarely the glial component progresses, giving an anaplastic ganglioglioma with more aggressive behaviour.
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI with epilepsy protocol to characterise the cystic and solid components
Video-EEG to confirm and localise the seizure focus
Histopathology demonstrating dysplastic ganglion cells and a glial component
BRAF V600E immunohistochemistry or molecular testing
CD34 immunostaining, which is frequently positive in glioneuronal tumours
Ki-67/MIB-1 index and grading assessment to detect anaplastic change
redFlags: Drug-resistant seizures with significant impact on quality of life
Features of anaplastic transformation such as rapid growth, marked enhancement or oedema
New focal neurological deficits suggesting progression
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent for the typical grade 1 tumour, with complete resection often curative and high rates of long-term seizure freedom. Anaplastic gangliogliomas are uncommon but behave more aggressively and may require adjuvant treatment; BRAF-targeted therapy is an option in selected higher-grade or unresectable cases.
pitfalls: Failing to identify the neuronal (ganglion cell) component and misclassifying the tumour as a pure glioma
Incomplete resection resulting in continued seizures
Overlooking anaplastic change in a previously indolent lesion
Not testing for BRAF V600E, which carries diagnostic and therapeutic relevance
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
Louis DN et al. The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System
management: Surgical resection of the contrast-enhancing tumor is the mainstay of treatment and is usually curative when gross total resection is achieved.
Most patients need no further therapy after a complete resection; the degree of anaplasia on histology determines prognosis.
Eloquent-region tumors remain resectable but are technically harder, aided by intraoperative microscope, computer-assisted navigation, and functional mapping.
Adjuvant radiotherapy is not required after gross total resection but is considered after subtotal resection, especially in eloquent locations.
Higher-grade histology generally warrants higher-intensity radiotherapy, particularly after subtotal resection.

Close imaging surveillance is a reasonable alternative to immediate postoperative radiotherapy after subtotal resection, reserving treatment for radiologic progression, particularly for lower-grade tumors.
Highly conformal radiotherapy techniques are preferred to limit long-term CNS toxicity given the young age of many patients.
Stereotactic radiosurgery is a reasonable option for limited recurrence after resection or at relapse.

Chemotherapy is not first-line; it is used mainly in children with subtotal resection and progression, and in adults as salvage after surgery and radiotherapy fail. No optimal regimen is established, and disease stabilization is considered a successful outcome.

In selected BRAF V600E-mutant tumors that are higher-grade or unresectable, BRAF-targeted therapy (a BRAF inhibitor with or without a MEK inhibitor) is a guideline-consistent option per NCCN, separate from DeVita's core recommendations.

Seizure control is a parallel treatment goal; patients with drug-resistant focal seizures should be evaluated through a dedicated epilepsy-surgery pathway with video-EEG localization, using antiepileptic drugs pending and after resection.
Follow-up centers on surveillance brain MRI to detect residual tumor, recurrence, or transformation to a higher-grade lesion, with re-grading if the tumor recurs or changes.
Any new diagnosis warrants referral to a neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team including neurosurgery and neuropathology.
Subtotal resection, eloquent location, higher-grade histology, or recurrence should prompt multidisciplinary discussion with radiation oncology.
